paragraphs: Assigning papers to reviewers involves more than matching expertise. Organizers may also want assignments that resist manipulation, protect reviewer anonymity, encourage diversity, and support evaluation of alternative assignments. Randomness can help with these goals, but the different motivations do not immediately identify a single best way to randomize the assignment process.

This paper introduces a practical randomized assignment method intended to work across those motivations. Its central question is how to produce useful randomness in a setting where reviewer expertise remains the main assignment objective. The contribution is a general-purpose approach, so organizers need not treat each reason for randomization as an entirely separate algorithm-design problem.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental comparisons showing improvements over currently deployed randomized assignment methods on several intuitive measures of randomness. Those results support the method’s usefulness across different assignment needs. The stated evidence concerns these randomness measures; it does not establish that every underlying goal, such as anonymity or resistance to malicious behavior, is automatically maximized.
neurips-2023-a-one-size-fits-all-approac.tldr: A practical paper-assignment method improves several measures of randomness to support multiple peer-review goals.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder pairs a network that generates data with one that infers latent representations. The structures of both networks affect performance, yet their depths are usually chosen before training. Finding a suitable fixed structure can require substantial tuning, and the abstract argues that existing regularization methods do not adequately address overfitting in deeper networks.

AdaVAE makes network structure part of Bayesian inference. It uses a beta process to model how many hidden layers the data justify in the encoding and decoding networks. A paired Bernoulli process supplies layer-wise dropout regularization. A scalable estimator then infers network structures together with latent variables, bringing architectural adaptation and representation learning into the same framework.

Experiments report prevention of overfitting in both shallow and deep VAEs, alongside state-of-the-art performance. The framework also works with different backbone networks and improves several VAE variants. These findings suggest that adapting depth to data can be a useful part of VAE training, rather than leaving structural decisions entirely to advance manual tuning.
neurips-2023-adavae-bayesian-structural-.tldr: AdaVAE jointly learns VAE depth and latent variables through Bayesian inference, with experiments showing reduced overfitting and improved performance.

paragraphs: Single-index models make predictions by applying an activation function to a single linear combination of inputs. This paper studies learning them in the agnostic setting, where the data need not follow such a model exactly. The authors handle arbitrary activations that are monotone and Lipschitz, meaning they preserve ordering and have a bounded rate of change.

The result removes two restrictions found in previous work: requiring an exactly realizable model or knowing the activation in advance. For the input distribution, it requires only bounded second moments. That allows a broader setting than earlier assumptions such as bounded inputs or anticoncentration, while retaining an explicit condition on the distribution.

The algorithm builds on omniprediction using predictors with calibrated multiaccuracy. Its analysis connects Bregman divergences, also described as matching losses, to familiar distance measures. The paper additionally establishes agnostic guarantees for GLMtron and logistic regression. Together, these contributions broaden the theoretical circumstances in which both the proposed approach and established algorithms can be justified.
neurips-2023-agnostically-learning-singl.tldr: The paper gives agnostic learning guarantees for single-index models with unknown monotone Lipschitz activations under bounded-second-moment assumptions.

paragraphs: Phylogenetic inference needs probabilistic models over possible tree structures. Designing such models is difficult because the alternatives are branching topologies rather than ordinary numerical vectors. Earlier approaches often described similarities between trees using hand-designed features, which require specialist knowledge and may restrict how flexibly the resulting model can approximate distributions over trees.

ARTree constructs a tree through a sequence of operations that add leaf nodes. At each stage, a graph neural network learns structural features and uses them to model the conditional distribution for the next operation. This autoregressive decomposition turns a distribution over complete trees into a series of distributions over construction steps, without relying on heuristic features.

The resulting model offers a rich family of tree distributions with straightforward sampling algorithms. The authors demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency on challenging real-data benchmarks involving tree-topology density estimation and variational Bayesian phylogenetic inference. The contribution is therefore both representational and computational: learned structural features support flexible probabilities, while sequential construction provides a practical way to draw trees.
neurips-2023-artree-a-deep-autoregressiv.tldr: ARTree learns flexible distributions over phylogenetic trees by using graph neural networks to model sequential leaf additions.

paragraphs: Pedestrian prediction becomes difficult when a person appears suddenly and there is little motion history to observe. BCDiff addresses this instantaneous prediction setting by generating both a possible unobserved past and a future trajectory. The idea is that these two estimates contain complementary information that can help improve each other despite the limited observations.

The framework couples two diffusion models through repeated mutual guidance. One generates future paths using the observed motion and the current estimate of the missing history. The other reconstructs that history using the observations and the predicted future. Because generated paths are particularly noisy early in this process, a learned gate balances their influence against the available observations.

This iterative exchange progressively refines both trajectory estimates. Experiments on ETH/UCY and Stanford Drone report significantly improved instantaneous prediction accuracy relative to related approaches. BCDiff also avoids an encoder, and the authors describe compatibility with existing trajectory predictors in principle. That compatibility is an architectural possibility, distinct from the demonstrated accuracy gains on the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2023-bcdiff-bidirectional-consis.tldr: BCDiff improves prediction from limited pedestrian observations by letting diffusion models jointly refine missing history and future paths.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can copy an expert’s actions through behavioral cloning or infer a reward through inverse reinforcement learning. Combining them is attractive, but optimizing a cloned policy against an inaccurate reward can undo the benefit of pretraining. This paper develops a connection between the cloned policy and its reward estimate to make subsequent refinement more coherent.

The derivation works in entropy-regularized reinforcement learning. By inverting the regularized policy update, the authors show how a behaviorally cloned policy can supply both a shaped reward and a hypothesis space for the critic. These connected components let reinforcement learning refine the copied behavior using the reward estimate, rather than starting from an independently specified reward.

The resulting workflow begins with behavioral cloning and continues with reinforcement learning using online or offline data. The authors report stable learning, little hyperparameter tuning, and scaling to high-dimensional and vision-based tasks compared with adversarial approaches. The significance is a relatively simple route from expert demonstrations to further policy improvement, grounded in the relationship established within the soft reinforcement-learning setting.
neurips-2023-coherent-soft-imitation-lea.tldr: Coherent Soft Imitation Learning connects a cloned policy to its reward and critic so reinforcement learning can refine the imitation.

paragraphs: People can teach robots through spoken instructions or demonstrations, but converting demonstrations into executable task code is challenging. Both the demonstrations and the resulting programs can be long and complex. Demo2Code addresses this difficulty by introducing an intermediate task specification that connects what was demonstrated with the code needed to perform it.

The framework uses two recursive stages. First, it repeatedly summarizes demonstrations into concise specifications. Second, it generates code from those specifications by recursively expanding functions. This gives the transformation an explicit intermediate representation: the first stage condenses the demonstration, while the second builds out the implementation. The authors describe the overall process as an extended chain-of-thought approach.

The paper evaluates Demo2Code on several robot-task benchmarks, including Robotouille, a new game benchmark featuring varied kitchen cooking tasks. The abstract establishes the framework’s design and evaluation scope without reporting comparative performance outcomes. Its central contribution is the structured route from demonstrations to programs, using a common specification to bridge two forms of task description that are difficult to map directly.
neurips-2023-demo2code-from-summarizing-.tldr: Demo2Code turns robot demonstrations into task code by recursively summarizing them into specifications and then expanding those specifications into functions.

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions provides group-level supervision: examples arrive in independently and identically distributed bags, and only each bag’s class frequencies are known. The learner nevertheless needs to classify individual examples well. This creates a mismatch between the information available during training and the individual-level loss that the learner ultimately wants to minimize.

EASYLLP addresses that mismatch through a debiasing method based on aggregate labels. It can operate with arbitrary loss functions and accurately estimate a model’s expected individual-level loss. The paper contrasts this approach with methods that train by matching bag proportions, examining differences in where the methods apply and the conditions under which they are optimal.

The authors integrate their method into empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent, with provable guarantees for performance on individual instances. Experiments across multiple datasets support the theory and illustrate circumstances where EASYLLP should do better or worse than earlier approaches. The contribution is thus a flexible way to train against the desired individual objective, with explicitly conditional comparative benefits.
neurips-2023-easy-learning-from-label-pr.tldr: EASYLLP uses aggregate class proportions to debias individual-level loss estimates and support standard learning methods with performance guarantees.

paragraphs: Adapting large vision transformers can be computationally expensive because backpropagation through their linear layers requires demanding matrix multiplications. This paper targets that part of fine-tuning directly. Its method, Low-rank BackPropagation via Walsh-Hadamard Transformation, or LBP-WHT, changes the space in which gradient computations are carried out during adaptation.

The central step projects the gradient into a low-rank space and performs backpropagation there. Matrix multiplications in that reduced space need less computation, which lowers the work required to adapt the model. The approach therefore focuses on the cost of the backward pass, offering a mechanism that the authors describe as complementary to many existing adaptation methods.

Experiments cover vision transformers and hybrid convolution-transformer models on multiple datasets. In the highlighted EfficientFormer-L1 adaptation experiment on CIFAR100, the authors report 10.4% higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art baseline with 9 MFLOPs less computation. This example demonstrates simultaneous accuracy and computational benefits in that setting. The paper also states that LBP-WHT can be combined with prior approaches for further performance improvements.
neurips-2023-efficient-low-rank-backprop.tldr: LBP-WHT reduces vision-transformer adaptation costs by computing backpropagation in a low-rank gradient space, with reported accuracy gains.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust prediction addresses uncertainty about the distribution on which a model will be used. For Wasserstein robust estimators, an especially useful guarantee links the training objective to true risk: with high probability, the robust objective itself is an upper bound. That makes the objective meaningful as a bound on performance beyond the training distribution.

Existing results supporting this relationship have faced several obstacles. Some deteriorate with dimension, some apply only in narrow settings, and others introduce additional error terms. This paper proves that exact upper-bound guarantees hold for general classes of models without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. The results can also cover distribution shifts at test time.

The authors further extend the guarantees to regularized Wasserstein robust problems. This matters because the theoretical relationship between the objective and true risk survives that change in formulation. The result remains a high-probability statement for the model classes and shifts covered by the theory; exactness describes the upper bound, rather than an assertion that the objective equals the true risk.
neurips-2023-exact-generalization-guaran.tldr: The paper proves exact high-probability risk bounds for broad classes of Wasserstein robust models, including regularized versions, without dimensionality-driven deterioration.

paragraphs: A trained neural network can rely on biased associations, such as linking hair color to gender. Correcting such behavior may require expensive bias labeling or retraining, and existing approaches may offer little explanation of where the bias comes from. Fast Model DeBias, or FMD, addresses identification, evaluation, and removal of bias within an already trained model.

FMD uses an explicit counterfactual concept to identify biased attributes and influence functions to quantify the influence of data samples. It then applies a machine-unlearning strategy using a small counterfactual dataset. The method needs only a small external dataset and changes a limited set of model parameters, without requiring access to the original training data.

Experiments on Colored MNIST, CelebA, and Adult Income report classification accuracy that is superior or competitive with state-of-the-art retraining methods, together with substantially less bias and lower debiasing cost. These findings support targeted post-training correction as a practical option when the original dataset is unavailable or too large to use. The reported outcome is reduced bias, rather than a claim that every possible bias is eliminated.
neurips-2023-fast-model-debias-with-mach.tldr: FMD uses counterfactual analysis and machine unlearning to reduce bias in trained models with limited updates and no original training-data access.

paragraphs: Federated learning can produce a shared model and then personalize it for each client’s local data. However, clients may differ in how far their preferred predictor lies from the shared model. A single hand-designed personalization strategy may therefore be unsuitable across the network. FedL2P treats the choice of personalization strategy as something the clients can learn together.

The method uses meta-networks that receive local data statistics and produce client-specific batch-normalization and learning-rate parameters. These parameters determine aspects of how the shared model is adapted locally. Training the meta-networks through federated learning lets the network collectively learn how to customize adaptation, while still conditioning each client’s strategy on its own data statistics.

Empirical results show improvements over a range of standard hand-crafted personalization baselines under both label shift and feature shift. The findings support learning the adaptation procedure itself as an additional source of benefit in federated systems. They also give a concrete implementation of client-specific strategies, rather than assuming that all clients should personalize with the same fixed settings.
neurips-2023-fedl2p-federated-learning-t.tldr: FedL2P federatively learns meta-networks that turn local data statistics into client-specific personalization settings.

paragraphs: Rényi differential privacy offers convenient rules for combining privacy guarantees across computations. Most mechanisms using it nevertheless randomize outputs represented by fixed finite-dimensional vectors. This paper extends the framework to outputs that are functions, whose spaces can be infinite-dimensional, making privacy analysis available for a broader kind of released object.

The authors develop functional Rényi differential privacy together with the tools needed to use it: Gaussian and subsampled Gaussian mechanisms, composition rules, and post-processing rules. They then apply the framework to functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. In their generative-model application, training is interpreted as repeatedly releasing loss functions with differential-privacy or Rényi differential-privacy guarantees.

Experiments report a significantly improved privacy–utility trade-off over existing alternatives, especially at epsilon equal to 0.2. This connects the theoretical extension to an observed benefit in private generative modeling. The key contribution is not merely a new accounting formula: it is a functional-output framework and a corresponding training interpretation that support a different way to construct private generative models.
neurips-2023-functional-renyi-differenti.tldr: Functional Rényi differential privacy extends privacy guarantees to function-valued outputs and enables a generative-training method with improved empirical privacy–utility trade-offs.

paragraphs: Data and model outputs can inhabit curved spaces, which makes extending privacy mechanisms beyond ordinary vector spaces important. This paper develops Gaussian differential privacy for Riemannian manifolds. The authors motivate this privacy definition through its central-limit properties and aim to work directly with manifold geometry rather than depend on tangent-space summaries.

Their construction uses a Riemannian Gaussian distribution based on distance along the manifold. Applying the Bishop–Gromov theorem, they establish Gaussian differential privacy on manifolds with bounded Ricci curvature. They also provide ways to calculate the privacy budget: a simple algorithm for any one-dimensional manifold and an MCMC-based algorithm for manifolds with constant curvature.

Simulations on the unit sphere show better utility than the previously proposed Riemannian Laplace mechanism when implementing Gaussian differential privacy. The findings support the value of a Gaussian mechanism that respects curved geometry. The scopes of the results are distinct: the privacy construction uses a curvature assumption, the general MCMC calculation targets constant curvature, and the reported utility comparison comes from sphere simulations.
neurips-2023-gaussian-differential-priva.tldr: The paper extends Gaussian differential privacy to curved spaces using a Riemannian Gaussian mechanism with curvature-dependent guarantees.

paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence can accurately describe its probability of being correct while still being difficult for a person to use. This paper examines that gap in decision support. For a broad class of utility functions, the authors identify data distributions where optimal decisions may require trusting lower-confidence predictions more than some higher-confidence predictions.

They introduce an alignment property relating the model’s confidence to the decision maker’s confidence in their own prediction. When that property holds, there is always an optimal policy whose trust in the model changes monotonically with its confidence. This makes the relationship easier to discover: optimal behavior need not require counterintuitive reversals in how confidence guides trust.

The paper also proves that multicalibration with respect to the person’s own confidence is sufficient for alignment. That is a sufficient route, not a claim that it is the only route. Experiments in a real AI-assisted decision setting validate the theoretical results and suggest that alignment may improve decisions. The broader contribution is to evaluate confidence in relation to the human using it.
neurips-2023-human-aligned-calibration-f.tldr: Aligning model confidence with a person’s own confidence guarantees an optimal monotone trust policy and may improve assisted decisions.

paragraphs: Frequency estimation asks how often each element appears in a data stream. Sketching algorithms provide probabilistic error guarantees for arbitrary inputs, while learning-augmented approaches try to improve estimates by exploiting the particular distribution being processed. One existing approach uses predictions of heavy hitters: elements expected to occur especially frequently in the stream.

This paper introduces a new algorithm that can improve on that earlier learning-based method even without predictions. The theoretical improvement holds in some parameter regimes, so the claim is conditional rather than a blanket advantage across all settings. Adding heavy-hitter predictions to the new algorithm reduces error further and improves on the state of the art.

The authors also report superior performance over prior approaches in every experiment they conducted. The results separate two sources of progress: a stronger underlying estimation algorithm and an additional benefit from learned predictions. This distinction matters when assessing learning-augmented methods, because improvements in the algorithm itself can change how much advantage should be attributed to the predictive component.
neurips-2023-improved-frequency-estimati.tldr: A new frequency estimator improves on an earlier prediction-based method in some regimes without predictions, and benefits further from heavy-hitter forecasts.

paragraphs: SATNet learns underlying rules from input-output examples using a differentiable MaxSAT solver. Its learned weights, however, do not directly provide rules a person can read or a formal tool can verify. This paper addresses that gap by developing a framework that extracts interpretable logical rules without requiring their structure to be specified in advance.

The proposed specification method, called maximum equality, permits conversion between SATNet’s weights and propositional rules expressed as a weighted MaxSAT formula. Once the formula is decoded, the authors apply verification techniques to compare it with ground-truth rules. This makes the learned rule system an explicit object that can be inspected and checked independently of SATNet’s original solver.

On stream-transformation and Sudoku problems, exact solvers using the decoded rules could achieve 100% accuracy, while the original SATNet produced incorrect solutions in many cases. The authors also formally verify functional equivalence between the decoded and ground-truth rules. These results show that, in the studied problems, reliable learned rules can support stronger outcomes when paired with exact solving and formal verification.
neurips-2023-learning-reliable-logical-r.tldr: A new SATNet specification decodes learned weights into readable logical rules that can be solved exactly and formally verified.

paragraphs: Facial-expression datasets contain many examples of some expressions and few of others. Overall accuracy on similarly imbalanced test data can conceal weak performance across expression classes. This paper aims to improve recognition of less common classes by looking for information about them throughout the training set, including examples labeled as common expressions.

The motivating idea is that an image can contain features relevant to multiple expressions. A surprise example, for instance, may also carry useful information about fear. The method uses rebalanced attention maps to encourage extraction of transformation-invariant information about minority expressions from all samples. It also introduces rebalanced smooth labels that adjust cross-entropy training using information about the imbalanced label distribution.

These two modules guide both which visual information the model extracts and how its training loss emphasizes minority classes. Experiments with different datasets and backbone networks show that the modules work together and achieve state-of-the-art performance on imbalanced facial-expression recognition. The contribution is a way to use potentially shared expression information, extending minority-class learning beyond the relatively few samples assigned those labels.
neurips-2023-leave-no-stone-unturned-min.tldr: Rebalanced attention and smooth labels help facial-expression models learn about rare expressions from both common-class and rare-class examples.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning estimates a value function, but its learning trajectory depends on interactions among state features, model parameters, and stochastic updates. This paper uses statistical-physics concepts to study typical learning curves for linear value-function approximators. Its focus is how error evolves during learning, including why progress can settle into extended plateaus.

The theory assumes Gaussian equivalence: averages over random trajectories are replaced by averages over Gaussian features with temporal correlations. The authors validate their assumptions on small Markov decision processes. Within this framework, they find that stochastic semi-gradient noise from sampling only some possible episodes produces substantial plateaus in value error, unlike the traditional gradient-descent dynamics used for comparison.

The analysis examines how feature structure, learning rate, discount factor, and reward function affect those dynamics and plateaus. It also studies how reducing the learning rate over time and reshaping rewards can improve them. The contribution is a set of analytical tools for understanding learning behavior under the stated approximation, connecting persistent error patterns to both representation choices and training choices.
neurips-2023-loss-dynamics-of-temporal-d.tldr: A statistical-physics analysis links error plateaus in linear temporal-difference learning to sampling noise and examines ways to improve the dynamics.

paragraphs: Skip connections and normalization layers are common architectural choices, but understanding their effects requires connecting individual layers to the behavior of the full loss landscape. This paper introduces a theoretical framework for doing that. It covers batch normalization, weight normalization, and skip connections within a common treatment of gradient-based optimization in deep networks.

The framework derives curvature and regularity properties of a multilayer loss from properties of its component layers. It explains how normalization and skip connections can make these properties hold globally. One application proves convergence to global optimal loss for a class of networks even when the optimum exists only at infinite parameter values, as can happen with cross-entropy.

A second application identifies a causal mechanism through which skip connections accelerate training. The authors test its predictions using ResNets on MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet. The significance is a link between architecture, landscape properties, and optimization behavior. The global-optimum theorem applies to the network class analyzed, while the experiments provide predictive evidence for the proposed acceleration mechanism.
neurips-2023-on-skip-connections-and-nor.tldr: A layer-based optimization framework explains effects of normalization and skip connections, including a mechanism for faster training.

paragraphs: Graph random features use random walks in approximating graph kernels. This paper improves their accuracy by changing how the walks are sampled together. Its central idea is to introduce negative correlations between walk lengths, using a procedure called antithetic termination to produce a more diverse collection of walks within the estimation algorithm.

The resulting quasi-Monte Carlo graph random features, or q-GRFs, require only a simple drop-in change. The authors prove that they produce lower-variance estimators of the 2-regularized Laplacian kernel under mild conditions. The guarantee applies across graph topologies, so it does not depend on restricting the graph to a particular structural family.

Experiments demonstrate accuracy improvements on several tasks, including efficient approximation of graph diffusion. These findings connect the variance analysis to practical estimation quality. The broader methodological lesson is that correlations between walks can be deliberately designed to improve an estimator. The paper establishes this benefit for its specified kernel and conditions, while introducing a sampling mechanism that may also be useful beyond the immediate application.
neurips-2023-quasi-monte-carlo-graph-ran.tldr: q-GRFs improve graph-kernel estimation by negatively correlating random-walk lengths, with lower-variance guarantees under mild conditions.

paragraphs: Evaluating recommendation explanations requires evidence about what users actually find explanatory. Existing datasets often lack labels from real users, cover only one type of explanation, or focus on a single aspect. REASONER addresses these gaps by collecting user-labeled explanation ground truths that span multiple modalities and aspects within a video-recommendation setting.

The researchers build a recommendation platform with carefully designed questions about explainability. Approximately 3,000 labelers from different backgrounds use the system, providing both behavioral data and answers to those questions. The paper describes how the dataset was constructed and analyzes its characteristics, making the collection process part of the contribution alongside the resulting data.

The project also implements ten established explainable-recommendation models in a unified library and uses them to build benchmarks for different explanation tasks. This supplies a shared basis for evaluating methods against the richer user feedback. The dataset, library, and documentation are released publicly. The contribution is evaluation infrastructure intended to advance explainable recommendation, rather than a demonstrated claim that explanations necessarily improve every user’s decisions.
neurips-2023-reasoner-an-explainable-rec.tldr: REASONER supplies real-user explanation labels across multiple modalities and aspects, alongside a shared library and recommendation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Decision trees can make learned control policies easier to interpret, but readable decisions do not by themselves establish system safety. This paper studies the difficulty of verifying systems controlled by such trees. It shows undecidability even with very simple dynamics and PSPACE-completeness for finite-horizon properties, establishing substantial computational obstacles to general verification.

For discrete-time systems, bounded model checking can address finite-horizon properties. Applying that route to continuous-time systems requires discretization, which weakens guarantees about the original system. The authors instead introduce an algorithm that works directly in continuous time. It exploits the tree’s decision structure to propagate a set-based approximation through the decision nodes.

Working with sets lets the verification procedure reason about collections of possible system states as the policy branches. The authors demonstrate the approach by verifying several decision-tree controllers distilled from neural-network policies for nonlinear systems. These demonstrations show that useful verification is possible despite the general hardness results. The central advance is exploiting the controller’s structure while avoiding the guarantee weakening associated with first discretizing continuous dynamics.
neurips-2023-safety-verification-of-deci.tldr: A structure-aware algorithm verifies decision-tree controllers directly in continuous time by propagating sets through their decision nodes.

paragraphs: Recommendation algorithms influence what producers choose to create, because producers want their content to be shown. This paper studies the resulting supply-side equilibria: stable patterns of content choices under those incentives. It represents content with multidimensional vectors and allows users to have different preferences, creating room for producers to specialize in different kinds of content.

Using a duality argument, the authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for specialization within their model. They then characterize equilibrium content distributions in concrete settings with two user populations. This moves the analysis beyond whether specialization is possible to what the collection of produced content looks like in particular modeled markets.

The paper also shows that specialization can allow producers to earn positive profit at equilibrium. In this sense, personalization can reduce market competitiveness by supporting differentiated producers. The result is a possibility established by the analysis, rather than a universal prediction about recommendation platforms. Its contribution is a theoretical account of how heterogeneous demand and multidimensional content interact with recommendation incentives to shape digital supply.
neurips-2023-supply-side-equilibria-in-r.tldr: A theoretical model characterizes when personalized recommendations encourage producer specialization and how that specialization can sustain positive profits.

paragraphs: The hippocampus supports memory and spatial representation through processes that depend on NMDA receptors. This paper investigates a computational analogy by designing a transformer activation function inspired by receptor dynamics. The proposed nonlinearity helps shift short-term working memory into long-term reference memory, producing behavior that resembles a form of biological memory consolidation.

The authors create a navigation task to assess the two memory functions. They then manipulate the activation function in a way intended to mimic magnesium gating of NMDA receptors. These manipulations disrupt long-term memory processes in the model, providing an experimental connection between the chosen nonlinear behavior and the transformer’s ability to establish reference memory.

The experiments suggest that place-cell-like functions and reference memory reside in the transformer’s feed-forward network layer, with nonlinearity driving those processes. This is evidence for a proposed correspondence between model components and hippocampal spatial-memory functions. The study uses that correspondence to explore memory consolidation computationally; the stated findings remain an experimentally supported analogy between the transformer and biological memory mechanisms.
neurips-2023-transformer-as-a-hippocampa.tldr: An NMDA-receptor-inspired activation gives transformers memory behavior resembling consolidation, with navigation experiments linking nonlinearity to long-term reference memory.
